d: Immortality, imperishability, freedom from death.

e.t: Immortality means the condition of not dying or being subject to death. It describes deathlessness rather than merely living for a long time. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears three times, all rendered “immortality.” Its meaning remains focused and consistent across its occurrences, while the surrounding verse explains how the idea is being used in each passage. The word appears in 1 Corinthians 15:53–54 and 1 Timothy 6:16.

d: Amos, son of Manasseh and father of Josiah, an ancestor of Jesus.

e.t: Amos is a personal name, referring to a man named in the genealogical records of the New Testament. It identifies an ancestor in Jesus’ recorded lineage, rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in two verses: twice in Matthew 1:10 and once in Luke 3:25. Its precise significance in those passages comes from the surrounding genealogy, but its basic function is simply to identify the person called Amos.

d: To make a mutual agreement; to confess, acknowledge, formally admit, give thanks to.
me: Verb, Imperfect, middle or passive depoNent, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to give thanks” or “to praise.” It describes expressing grateful acknowledgment toward God or another recipient, rather than merely feeling thankful inwardly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 2:38, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains an outward response of gratitude or praise, directed toward the one being honored.

d: A freedman, one who has been a slave but has been manumitted by his master.

e.t: This word means “freedman,” referring to a person who has been released from slavery. It is a noun that identifies someone by a former condition of bondage and a present condition of freedom. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 7:22. That reference marks its only recorded occurrence in this corpus; the word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding text.

d: Perplexity, anxiety, doubt.

e.t: Perplexity describes a troubled state in which a person cannot readily understand a situation or determine what to do. It expresses bewilderment and uncertainty rather than a settled conclusion. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Luke 21:25, and is rendered “perplexity” there. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the experience of being deeply puzzled or at a loss.

d: A beryl, a precious stone of various colors, the best known being sea-green.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “beryl,” the name of a particular gemstone. It functions as a noun naming the stone, rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament corpus, in Revelation 21:20. Its lexical meaning identifies the stone itself; the surrounding verse determines how that stone is being used in the passage. The English rendering is consistently “beryl.”

d: A generation; if repeated twice or with another time word, practically indicates infinity of time.

e.t: This word means “generation” or “generations,” referring to people belonging to one period or to successive family lines. It is a noun used in the Greek New Testament for a particular generation of people and, in some settings, generations viewed across time. The word occurs 43 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that it is used broadly in discussions of ancestry, time, and the people living in a given era.

d: To scatter, winnow, disperse, waste.

e.t: This word means “to scatter,” describing the act of spreading people or things apart so they are no longer together. It can also describe people who “were scattered,” emphasizing the resulting condition of being dispersed. The word occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, showing a recurring idea of separation or spreading in different settings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: Thither, there, at that place.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “there,” pointing to a particular place or location. It functions as an adverb, directing attention away from the speaker or current setting toward another place already understood from the surrounding sentence or passage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding context, but its basic role remains simple: it identifies a destination or location without naming that place itself.

d: Chosen out, elect, choice, select, sometimes as of those chosen out by God for the rendering of special service to Him (of the Hebrew race, particular Hebrews, the Messiah, and the Christians).

e.t: This word describes those who are “elect” or “select”—those marked out as selected rather than treated as part of an undifferentiated group. Its central idea is distinction by selection, identifying people or things regarded as the selected ones. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 22 times, making it a recurring description rather than a term limited to one passage. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but “elect” and “select” express its basic meaning.

d: To mock, ridicule.

e.t: This word means “mocked” or “to mock”: to treat someone with contempt through scornful words or behavior. It describes an act of ridicule rather than simple disagreement or criticism. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 13 times, including passages describing people being mocked. Its repeated use in the Gospel accounts shows a clear action of humiliating or deriding someone. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the people involved.

d: To engrave, imprint.
me: Verb, peRfect, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “to be engraved” or “to engrave,” describing something marked or written firmly into a surface. Its basic picture is writing that is impressed so it remains inscribed rather than merely spoken or temporarily displayed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 3:7. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on engraving or being engraved.

d: (a) an exit, going out, departure from a place; the exodus, (b) death.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “departure” or “exodus,” referring to the act of leaving or going out. It is a noun that identifies a departure rather than the person who leaves or the place being left. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 9:31, Hebrews 11:22, and 2 Peter 1:15. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To travel, journey (to).
me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Participle, Genitive, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to come,” “to come to,” or “to come/go to.” It is a verb describing movement toward a place or destination. In ordinary Bible usage, it focuses on someone arriving or going toward something rather than remaining where they are. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 8:4, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

d: Dangerous, likely to fall.

e.t: This word describes something dangerous or unsteady—something that cannot be considered safe or dependable. It is an adjective, so it characterizes a situation, condition, or circumstance as risky. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:9. The surrounding verse context would determine exactly what is being described there, but the word itself points to present danger or instability rather than safety.

d: To do good deeds, perform kind service, benefit.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to do good” or “to do good to,” describing beneficial action toward others. It focuses on actively helping or treating someone well rather than merely having good intentions. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 10:38. Its exact force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is purposeful goodness expressed through action.

d: Devout, pious, God-fearing.

e.t: This word means “godly”: it describes someone whose character and conduct are devoted to God. It presents a person as recognizing God’s authority and seeking to live in a way that honors him. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 9:31. The word’s basic emphasis is the person’s God-directed character, while the surrounding verse determines how that description functions in its sentence.

d: Jairus, a Jewish ruler of the synagogue.

e.t: Jairus is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs twice, in Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is chiefly identifying the individual who bears it; the surrounding verse and passage provide the details about him. The name is rendered consistently as “Jairus” in the available English translations.

d: Judah, Judas, Jude.

e.t: This word is a proper name rendered “Judah” or “Judea.” It identifies a biblical name in the Greek New Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. English translations use these two approved forms for the word, so its precise reference is determined by the surrounding verse. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in two verses. The word itself contributes the name; the broader significance comes from the person or place identified in its context.

d: To bind up, bandage.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to bandage”: to cover and bind a wound with material so it can be cared for. It functions as a verb, describing an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 10:34. The word’s basic sense is practical and concrete, referring to the act of treating an injury rather than expressing an abstract idea.

d: Danger, peril, risk.

e.t: This word means “danger”: a threatening or hazardous situation that may bring harm. It functions as a noun, naming a real risk or peril rather than an emotion or an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, with its usage concentrated in two verses. Its central idea remains straightforward: circumstances that place someone in jeopardy or expose them to serious harm.

d: A feasting, reveling, carousal.

e.t: This word means “orgy,” referring to wild, excessive revelry marked by drunken or immoral celebration. It describes behavior that belongs to a life ruled by uncontrolled pleasure rather than disciplined conduct. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: in Romans, Galatians, and 1 Peter. Its repeated association with other sinful practices shows that it names a serious form of indulgence, not ordinary joy, fellowship, or celebration.

d: Lois, grandmother of Timothy.

e.t: Lois is a personal name referring to a woman identified in the Greek New Testament. It appears once, in 2 Timothy 1:5, and is rendered “Lois.” Because the word is a name rather than a descriptive title or action word, its basic meaning is the person it names. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain how she is presented there; the name itself does not supply that contextual detail.

d: To engage in battle, fight; hence: to strive, contend, dispute.
me: Verb, Imperfect, middle or passive depoNent, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means to fight or quarrel. It describes active conflict, whether people are engaging in an open dispute or contending against one another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse. The word can therefore describe more than physical combat; it may also refer to hostile disagreement or strife between people. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is conflict expressed through fighting or quarrelling.

d: (a) to take a share (part) of, share in, partake of, (b) to take after (later) or take instead.
me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, second Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to partake” or “to share in”—to receive or participate in something together with others. It can describe sharing in food, benefits, experiences, or what is provided. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Acts, 2 Timothy, and Hebrews. Its broad sense is participation: someone does not merely observe what is happening but has a portion in it or receives from it. The exact emphasis in any verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as being shared or received.

d: To nod, make a sign, beckon.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Genitive, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek verb means “to motion”—to communicate or direct something by a gesture or signal. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in John 13:24 and Acts 24:10. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of signaling or indicating through a motion.

d: To nod in sleep, to be drowsy, slumber.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to become drowsy” or “to doze.” It describes a person becoming sleepy or drifting into light sleep, rather than deliberately choosing to rest. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 25:5 and 2 Peter 2:3. Its basic meaning remains the same in both occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation being described. It is therefore a straightforward word for the onset or experience of sleepiness.

d: To howl, lament loudly, cry aloud, bewail.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to wail”: to express intense grief or distress through a loud, sorrowful cry. It is an action word, describing what a person does rather than naming the feeling itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 5:1. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular situation there, but the word’s basic meaning remains an anguished expression of sorrow.

d: To stir up, incite, urge on.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means “to incite”: it describes stirring someone or a group to action, often by urging them on. As a verb, it points to causing a response rather than merely describing a feeling or opinion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 13:50. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is causing others to act.

d: Confidence, trust, reliance.

e.t: This word means “confidence”: a firm sense of trust or assurance. It describes a person’s settled reliance rather than uncertainty or hesitation. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times, all in six verses, and is rendered “confidence.” Its use includes confidence directed toward God, confidence about people, and confidence in one’s own standing or abilities. The surrounding sentence determines what the confidence rests on, but the central idea remains firm trust or assurance.

d: A rock, ledge, cliff, cave, stony ground.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “a rock” or “rocks,” referring to a solid mass or formation of stone. It is a noun used for literal rocky objects and places. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek New Testament, across 14 verses, so its basic meaning is consistently connected with stone or rock. Its wider significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding words and context, but the central idea remains something solid, rocky, and enduring.

d: A cause of stumbling, offense, shock.

e.t: This word means “stumbling” or “stumbling block”—something associated with tripping or causing someone to stumble. It can describe an obstacle that interferes with a person’s progress rather than a physical act alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 6:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is an impediment or cause of stumbling.

d: A rod, staff, staff of authority, scepter.

e.t: The word means “rod,” referring to a physical staff-like object. In the Greek New Testament, it names the object itself rather than an action or quality. Its particular significance depends on the surrounding passage, since a rod may be mentioned in different settings. This word occurs 12 times in 11 New Testament verses, from Matthew through Revelation, and its central meaning remains the same: a rod.

d: Shem, a son of Noah.

e.t: Shem is a personal name, referring to a person named Shem rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 3:36, and is rendered “Shem.” Because this word functions as a name, its basic meaning is identification: it distinguishes one individual from others. The particular significance of Shem in Luke 3:36 belongs to that passage’s surrounding genealogy and context, while the word itself simply names him.

d: A tent-maker.

e.t: This word refers to a tentmaker, a person who makes tents. It is a noun describing someone by this occupation, rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Acts 18:3. The word’s basic meaning remains focused and concrete: a worker whose trade is making tents. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the person’s occupation.

d: To oppress, bend together.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iMperative, second, Singular

e.t: This word means “to be bent over” or “to bend.” It describes the action of curving downward rather than remaining upright, and it functions as an action word in the Greek New Testament. It occurs once in that corpus, in Romans 11:10. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise force of the action in that passage must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains physical bending or being caused to bend.

d: To happen, occur, meet.

e.t: This word means “to happen”—to take place or come about. It describes an event as something that has occurred, is occurring, or may occur, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it appears eight times, including uses rendered “happened” and “happen.” Its basic focus is the fact of an event taking place, without by itself explaining whether that event is good, bad, expected, or unexpected. The surrounding sentence and passage determine those details.

d: A putting together in the mind, hence: understanding, practical discernment, intellect.

e.t: This word means “understanding”: the ability to grasp meaning, recognize how things fit together, and respond with insight. It describes more than merely hearing or knowing words; it points to clear comprehension. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times and is used for human understanding as well as understanding connected with God’s truth and purposes. The word appears in passages concerning wise answers, learning, spiritual insight, and comprehending what has been taught. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: Art, skill, trade, craft.

e.t: This word means “skill,” referring to the ability or expertise needed to perform a craft or skilled task. It describes practiced competence rather than merely possessing an object or holding a position. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in separate verses: twice in Acts and once in Revelation. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the ability to carry out skilled work.

d: Timon, one of the seven original deacons at Jerusalem.

e.t: Timon is a personal name, referring to a man named Timon rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, the name occurs once, at Acts 6:5. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this entry explains the name itself, not Timon’s particular role or significance in that passage. The English rendering preserves the name as “Timon.”

d: To increase exceedingly or beyond measure.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to grow more and more” or “to increase.” It describes growth that continues and becomes greater, rather than a fixed or merely existing condition. In ordinary Bible reading, it points to something developing in extent or strength over time. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in 2 Thessalonians 1:3. The reference identifies its only occurrence, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific subject and context.

d: (literal: to make room, hence) (a) to have room for, receive, contain, (b) to make room for by departing, go, make progress, turn myself.

e.t: This word means “to go” or “to make room for.” It can describe movement from one place to another, or the availability of space for something or someone. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 10 times across 9 verses, showing that it serves both a movement sense and a room-making sense. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.
